[MUQATIL:15:29-31/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God fashioned Adam's creation, breathed into him, and commanded the angels to prostrate to him.
[TAB-FULL:v14p66/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God says that when He had formed and proportioned Adam and breathed life into him, Adam became a living human.
[TAB-FULL:v14p66/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The angels' prostration was an act of greeting and honor, not worship.
[TAB-FULL:v14p66/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that successive groups of angels refused to prostrate and were burned by fire; a later group obeyed, while Iblis remained among the earliest unbelievers.
[NAHHAS:v2p379/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ساجدين is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.
[SULAMI:v1p353#4/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو عثمان | reports | Abu Uthman says that after God distinguishes Adam through qualities of the spirit and repentance, the angels must stop disputing and submit to the command to prostrate.
[SULAMI:v1p353#4/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti says Adam's knowledge, the spirit's knowledge, and its will are all constituted by God's knowing, knowledge, and willing; the spirit wills what God wills among its loves.
[SULAMI:v1p353#4/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The angels first saw Adam's form but not the spirit's divine attribution, repentance, knowledge of names, or glimpse of the unseen; when God disclosed these marks of special friendship and nearness, they prostrated.
[SULAMI:v1p353#4/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti distinguishes Adam's spirit from other things by the completion of its form and the special divine attribution; it is brought near, enabled to know God's rule, effaced, and returned to God by indication.
[SULAMI:v1p353#4/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | The spirit is stripped of independent action and speech: it is adorned by God's creation, takes on His character, speaks through Him, and understands through His indication.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi glosses forming Adam as shaping and proportioning his figure into a human form.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Nafkh means causing air to flow into something.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The spirit is a subtle body by which the body lives; al-Wahidi defers fuller discussion to the verse asking about the spirit. | mentions 17:85
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | God attributes Adam's spirit to Himself as an honor and distinction, in the sense of a possession attribution.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Fa-qaʿu is an imperative derived from falling.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p601/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi and the exegetes say the angels prostrated to Adam as a greeting of respect, not as an act of worship; al-Wahidi refers to discussions of its manner and greeting-prostration elsewhere. | mentions 12:100
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:15:29/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God fashioned Adam and breathed into him a spirit created by God.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:15:29/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The prostration before Adam was a greeting.
[DAMGHANI:v1p493/r3] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | وقع can mean fell down prostrate.
[JISHUMI:v6p3945/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Blowing is the act of sending air into something.
[JISHUMI:v6p3945/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Taswiya is setting things to an equal measure or form, and can also mean making them equal in judgment or another respect.
[JISHUMI:v6p3946/r27] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | One explanation says God completed Adam's creation and perfected him; another says He fashioned and completed his form.
[JISHUMI:v6p3946/r28] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The blowing is a figurative expression for giving life; the spirit is attributed to God because He alone can do this, or as an honorific attribution.
[JISHUMI:v6p3946/r29] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو القاسم | reports | Abū al-Qāsim says the prostration was a greeting, not worship; worship belongs to God, while the greeting was for Adam.
[JISHUMI:v6p3946/r30] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī says Adam was the direction toward which the angels prostrated, as the Kaaba is a direction of prayer.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p380/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Taswiyah means shaping Adam's form and completing his creation.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p380/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The spirit is a subtle body by which humans live; it made Adam living, and its attribution to God is honorific.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p380/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The commanded prostration was a greeting, not worship.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | The verb supports the view that the angels’ prostration was the familiar physical act, not merely deference, submission, or a gesture.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعض الناس | rejects | Some people explain the angels’ prostration as deference, submission, or a gesture rather than the familiar prostration; the author rejects this.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو الأخزر الحماني | reports | Abū al-Akhzar al-Ḥammānī’s line says that a head ‘prostrated,’ a poetic parallel suggesting the familiar physical act.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | Al-Ṭabarī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that God created angels who refused Adam’s prostration and were burned, then created another group who obeyed except Iblīs, who was among the first.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | God announced an astonishing creation to angels made of light and subtle beings: He would make a living, bodily creature with skin from clay.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ‘I fashioned him’ means that God completed and perfected Adam until his parts were properly ordered.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The possessive phrase attributes a created, owned spirit to its Creator and Owner; ‘spirit’ here is a generic class term.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p359#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ‘Fall’ comes from waqaʿa/yqaʿu, with the qāf opened because of the following guttural letter.
[TABRISI:15:28-33/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Sawwaytuhu means completing Adam's creation, or proportioning his form.
[TABRISI:15:28-33/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Breathing is causing air to flow; God caused the spirit to flow into Adam, and attributing it to Himself honors Adam as an ownership attribution.
[TABRISI:15:28-33/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The spirit is attributed to God as an honorific and an attribution of ownership.
[TABRISI:15:28-33/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī glosses the command as falling in prostration before Adam.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p400/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | When God has fashioned Adam, He has proportioned his form and completed his creation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p400/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The spirit is the life-giving human spirit, whose nature is unknown; its attribution to God honors Adam and denotes ownership, and its entry is called breathing because it flows through the body like wind.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p400/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Fa-qaʿū is an imperative form of the verb meaning to fall.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After recounting the creation of the first human as evidence for a powerful, choosing God, the passage turns to God's command that the angels prostrate; all obeyed except Iblis.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One explanation of God's forming Adam is shaping him in human form and bodily constitution.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second explanation is arranging Adam's bodily parts through balanced temperaments and proportioned mixtures, as the verse about the human being formed from mixed fluid says. | mentions 76:2
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Blowing is moving air through cavities in another body; the wording appears to imply that spirit is air, though the full account of spirit is deferred to 17:85. | mentions 17:85
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God attributes Adam's spirit to Himself as a mark of honor and distinction.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The exegetical question is whether the prostration was truly directed to Adam or whether Adam served as its qibla.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The command may have addressed all heavenly angels, only some angels, or the angels of earth.
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | Some deny that the highest angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, since the verse about those near God says they prostrate to God alone. | mentions 7:206
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The general wording commands prostration to Adam, but the specific statement that the angels prostrate to God alone takes precedence over that general wording. | mentions 7:206
[RAZI-FULL:v19p144#3/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The fāʾ in the command indicates immediate succession after God's forming and breathing the spirit, with no intervening delay.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p171#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Quran describes God's breathing into Mary and into Adam; Razi notes that the wording concerning Jesus can grammatically refer to Mary because Jesus was in her womb. | mentions 66:12, 15:29

[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl says the angels were superior to Adam and God tested them by commanding prostration to him, exposing them to great reward; this is the Muʿtazilite position.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another view says the angels were ordered to prostrate to God in Adam’s presence, with Adam serving as their qibla.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | I have proportioned it means that God formed and shaped Adam’s creation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Blowing means passing air into something.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The spirit is a subtle body; God customarily creates life in the body together with it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The spirit is a created thing attributed to its Creator for honor, like God’s earth, sky, house, camel, and month.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The phrase is comparable to روح منه in 4:171, explained earlier under al-Nisāʾ. | mentions 4:171
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | In al-Tadhkira the author cited reports indicating that the spirit is a subtle body and that nafs and rūḥ name one referent; he plans to return to the subject.
[QURTUBI-FULL:15:28-29/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Those who identify the spirit with life understand the phrase as meaning that God put life into Adam.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:15:28-29/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | To shape Adam is to proportion his form and prepare it for the spirit.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:15:28-29/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The spirit first attaches to subtle vapor from the heart, receives life, and travels through the arteries and body; its relation to the body is called blowing because air passes into another body’s cavity.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:15:28-29/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The spirit’s attribution to God follows the explanation given in al-Nisāʾ. | mentions 4:171

[NASAFI-FULL:v2p240#9/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | When God completed and formed Adam, He prepared him to receive the spirit.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p240#9/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The spirit means that God gave Adam life; there was no literal blowing, which is figurative, and the possessive phrase marks special attribution.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p240#9/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Waqaʿa means fall, here to prostrate; the fāʾ makes the command the answer to idhā, showing a command may precede its time of action.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p476/r18] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Sawwaytuhu means completing Adam's creation with precision and making its parts proportionate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p476/r19] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “I breathed into him of My spirit” means God created life in Adam; no literal blowing or breathed object is intended, only a figurative image for imparting life.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p476/r20] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The spirit is attributed to God as an honorific, like God's House and she-camel, or because God directly creates the spirit and places it where He wills.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p476/r21] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The phrase waqaʿū lahu means that they fell to the ground.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p220/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God's fashioning means completing and adjusting Adam, preparing him almost fully for the imparting of spirit.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p220/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Breathing the spirit means creating life in Adam, figuratively like fire catching in a wick through blowing; attributing the spirit to God honors it, and its highest excellence is making a knower act humbly.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p220/r13] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The angels were commanded to prostrate in honor of Adam; falling as if involuntarily conveys their immediate and easy obedience.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Outwardly, God shaped Adam in human form; the breath means air entering a body able to retain it and is metaphor for creating life.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | There is no literal breath or breathed substance: the phrase describes the Creator’s relation to the created and manifestation of His attribute and act in Adam.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الشيخ عز الدين | reports | Shaykh ʿIzz al-Dīn says breath signifies ignition of the soul’s light in a receptive place; the physical image cannot apply to God, but its effect can be named for its cause.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الشيخ عز الدين | reports | For ʿIzz al-Dīn, the active cause is divine generosity, spring of existence and power, while the receiver is the balance created by shaping.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الشيخ عز الدين | reports | He likens the receptive quality to a polished mirror that takes the image facing it; the soul appears when the embryo reaches balance.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Persian couplet compares the heart to a polished mirror capable of receiving limitless forms, and says polishers immediately see beauty.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God adds the breath to Himself because He personally shaped Adam with His holy hands and breathed directly, without intermediary.
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The attributed spirit is the breath of the All-Merciful and shadowy existence, linked to 25:45. | mentions 25:45
[BURSEVI:v4p305#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | This direct divine breath into Adam’s shaped form entails knowledge of all the Names, both gracious and majestic.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Faqaʿū is the imperative of waqaʿa and requires falling prostrate, not merely bowing, in obedience and as honor for Adam, who displays divine wonders like a qibla.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Bursevī recounts a true dream of his shaykh: he remained pure to his last breath, then performed ablution at a spring after death, ascended to heaven, and returned to pray at his own funeral.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | In the dream, the shaykh answers that earthly intellect and perception remain after death.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Bursevī infers that ablution is invalidated at death agony, grounding the sounder view that a deceased person must be washed; the complete believer remains pure, since hadath is not impurity.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The complete person is washed as an imperfect person because outwardly he lacks ablution and follows the imperfect in worldly appearances.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Intellect, faith, sainthood, and similar qualities belong to the spirit and therefore do not change at death.
[BURSEVI:v4p306#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The perfected spirit’s funeral prayer signifies that in reality the perfected person is both prostrating and prostrated to; people’s prayer echoes angels’ prostration to Adam while remaining supplication at the legal level.
[BURSEVI:v4p307/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads shaping as making Adam fit to receive the divine breath; the possessive spirit marks its special nearness and rank in the highest heavenly realm (50:16). | mentions 50:16
[BURSEVI:v4p307/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | The spirit descends through angels, whose luminous qualities fold into it like starlight into sunlight; it then passes through jinn and devils, taking their traits, and through animals, receiving senses and powers.
[BURSEVI:v4p307/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | The spirit attaches to Adam’s form, molded by God with gentleness and severity and prepared for manifestation; God commands prostration because of Adam’s perfected form, knowledge, and capacity for disclosure.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī takes the making level as bringing Adam to balance and full readiness to receive the spirit.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An alternative explanation is that God formed Adam in human shape and the human constitution.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | In ordinary usage, blowing means sending air from the mouth or elsewhere into a cavity able to hold and fill with it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Here blowing figuratively represents imparting actual life to receptive matter; no literal blowing occurs.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | reports | Al-Ghazālī explains the blowing image as a cause standing for its effect: prepared clay is like a wick ignited by fire, though the resulting life need not resemble the cause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام وجماعة من المحققين | reports | Al-Ghazālī and other verificationists describe the spirit as an immaterial substance, neither body nor bodily accident, and neither inside nor outside the body or joined to it or separate from it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جماعة من المحققين | reports | Their first proof says universal intelligible forms cannot inhere in a point, which would always be receptive and make every

 point-bearing body rational, or in divisible matter, which would divide the forms.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشيخ | reports | The Sheikh's self-knowledge proof says self-awareness cannot depend on a second equal image, which duplicates the self; direct presence to oneself instead implies a self-subsisting, nonbodily intellect.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p36#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أفلاطون | reports | Plato argues that the mind can distinguish imagined nonexistent forms; the small body cannot contain these vast forms, and surrounding air is neither part of the body nor an instrument of the soul.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A fourth proof argues that if perceptions inhered in a body, one part could know while another part was ignorant of the same thing at the same time.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A fifth proof rejects an embodied soul: it would always perceive its organ, never perceive it, or perceive it only sometimes; each fails, and an image of the organ would either duplicate itself or require an immaterial soul.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī says the Imam's al-Mabāḥith presents twelve proofs, including arguments already given, then relies on a further argument.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام | reports | The Imam's favored argument starts from our self-evident awareness that we are the same person as before: the self is neither the changing body nor an accident dependent on it, so it is an immaterial substance.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام | reports | He adds that animals may know their own identities, but do not know that their present selves are those that existed earlier, so the immaterial human self need not belong to every animal.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p37/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī introduces another proof: one entity in a person is the perceiver for every kind of perception and every object perceived.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The unified perceiver cannot be the body itself, a quality in every body part, or a quality in just one part: we do not find every part perceiving or one all-purpose perceiving organ.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جمهور أهل السنة | reports | The Sunni majority instead holds that the spirit is a subtle body differing from other bodies in essence and qualities, dwelling in the body like oil in olives or fire in coal; al-Juwaynī adopts this view.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · اللقاني | reports | Al-Laqqānī describes the spirit as a luminous, self-living, subtle upper body permeating the organs like rosewater in a rose; it does not decay, and its presence is life while separation is death.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Nor can the perceiver be a subtle body hidden in an organ, since no such location is experienced; because we directly know ourselves as perceivers, an unknown body's identity cannot explain that self-awareness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | These arguments conclude that the common subject of perception is neither body nor body-dependent, but an immaterial substance.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الذاهبون إلى التجرد | reports | Those who hold the spirit immaterial say its bond with the body resembles an instinctive, divinely inspired lover's attachment to the beloved and governs and directs the body while it remains receptive.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | reports | Al-Ghazālī says the possessive attribution 'My spirit' reflects creation without an intermediary that serves as origin or matter, or serves as an honorific attribution.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | reports | Al-Ghazālī compares this attribution to the sun saying it gave earth its light: the light is of the sun's kind, though extremely weak by comparison; the spirit's spacelessness and universal knowledge mark a likeness that warrants the attribution.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī answers that two spaceless beings can remain distinct through their essences, just as different qualities in one body, or the same quality at different times, are distinct without separate places.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | He rejects the objection that being outside place is uniquely divine: God's unique attribute is self-subsistence, while everything else depends on and borrows its existence from Him.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p38/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المناوي | reports | Al-Munāwī says the factions' many rational speculations on the spirit yielded no sure result; Ibn Jamāʿa held that none of the more than a thousand views is sound.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some identify the human being with the visible bodily frame and make the spirit an accident inhering in it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī answers that a spirit's being bodily does not make every body a spirit: it is spirit through a special divine property and is alive in itself, so no infinite regress of spirits follows.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The animal spirit is a subtle vaporous body generated from subtle humors, arising from the heart's left cavity and spreading through the body as the rational soul's vehicle of control.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المتأخرين من المعاصرين | reports | Some later contemporaries ascribed that view to the majority of theologians and used it, together with the impossibility of uniting prior states, to argue that a servant does not create his own acts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام | prefers | The Imam rejects identifying the person with the visible frame and approves the majority position, since bodily parts continually change while the person remains the same from beginning to end.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جمهور المتكلمين | reports | The majority reason that the enduring self cannot be the body, whose parts continually wither, grow, increase, diminish, mature, and dissolve; what changes completely is not the persistent person.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المحققون | reports | Among accounts of the self, the most satisfactory concise one says it consists of bodily components pervading the frame like water in a rose or oil in sesame; the discerning add that these components differ in nature from the frame's changing parts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المحققون | reports | On this bodily-soul account, its own persistent particles are luminous and alive; they animate the changing frame, then separate at its corruption for the realm of holiness if blessed or afflictions if wretched.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صاحب الهياكل | reports | The author of al-Hayākil argues that we never lose awareness of ourselves although we sometimes forget body parts; since a whole is known only through its parts, the self is beyond the body.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الجلال | reports | Al-Jalāl objects that this proves only that the soul is beyond the visible body, not that it is immaterial; it could still be a subtle body.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p39/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qāḍī says most theologians regard the spirit as an accident identical with life; Ustadh Abū Isḥāq adopts this despite the resulting accident-in-an-accident problem.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Another account identifies the spirit with the balanced temperament of the heart's blood.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | reports | His argument against preexistent souls says one soul shared by all would make everyone share the same knowledge and ignorance, while dividing one immaterial soul into many is impossible.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | reports | If preexistent souls were already many, their individuation would require differences in essence, necessary properties, or accidents; shared species rules out the first two, while accidents cannot precede the body that supplies matter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Some verificationists distinguish a subtle spirit permeating the body from a noble divine-command spirit that shines upon it and may give it life, perception, and luminosity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | They take the spirit meant by the question in 17:85 to be the second, divine-command spirit. | mentions 17:85
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | In this terminology, the first spirit is the human self, while the second is the rational self; the immaterial substance described as neither body nor bodily is the spirit in this latter sense.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Scholars disagree whether souls originate before or after bodies.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · حجة الإسلام | prefers | Al-Ghazālī holds that souls arise when bodies become ready to receive them, like an image appearing when a mirror is polished, although the image's source existed earlier; Aristotle and his followers also held this.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | An objection cites a report that God created spirits two thousand years before bodies; no chain or grading is supplied here.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī reports Ghazālī's answer that the spirits in this report are angels and the bodies are the world's vast bodies, such as the Throne, Kursī, and heavens, rather than human bodies.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p40/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The argument likens hu

man spirits to a lamp kindled from an immense fire covering the world, the last spirit among the angels, and human bodies to the vastly larger cosmic bodies.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي صلى الله عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | A Prophetic saying presents Muhammad as the first prophet in creation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The first objection to the prior-soul proof asks why one preexistent soul could not later multiply; the reply distinguishes connected divisible unity from unity in general, since a universal affirmative does not convert.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي صلى الله عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | Another Prophetic saying says Muhammad was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The explanation reads “created” in the first-prophet report as predestination, not actual existence: ends precede their means in design but follow them in existence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The architect's completed house is first as a design and last to exist; preparatory work serves it, just as first thought is last in the finished work.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Human creation aims at knowing the happiness of nearness to God, attainable only through prophetic instruction; prophethood's completion in Muhammad is the goal, making him first in the plan and last in historical existence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The report about Adam is taken to indicate that Adam was made to yield the purest descendant, with selection continuing through generations until Muhammad.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The discussion distinguishes an ideal existence in the planner's mind from external existence; God's prior decree is inscribed on the Preserved Tablet before realization, as an architect's design precedes a house.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The divine Pen conveys forms to the receptive Tablet according to eternal knowledge; neither need be physical, and they may be understood as spiritual teacher and learner.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p41/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The Pen and Tablet analogy is linked to 96:4, “He taught by the pen,” and the passage concludes that Muhammad preceded others in ideal existence, not actual existence. | mentions 96:4
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المعترضون | reports | The objection says both camps hold souls survive bodily separation and are distinguished by accidents; for potential souls, attachment to different bodies may itself individuate them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If a soul divided, its parts would differ from the whole; essential difference makes the parts already distinct, while nonessential difference requires unequal magnitude and thus divisibility.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Even granting that an immaterial simple soul cannot split after unity, the individual determinations arise only after bodily attachment, so each soul is originated as an individual.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المعترضون | reports | An objection asks why distinction must depend on a qualifying attribute; Alusi answers by the same reasoning used for individuation itself.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المعترضون | reports | An objection proposes that souls differ through constitutive qualities; Alusi says it is not self-evident that each soul-kind must have several individuals, and one individual per kind would complete the argument.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The argument does not depend on disproving transmigration: plurality within one species shows individuality is not essential, but caused by relation to a particular body, so the soul is not individuated before that body.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | An inhering accident cannot distinguish a soul, since its inherence presupposes the soul is already distinguished; individuation must depend on the receptacle or body, while theologians also reject such accounts by infinite regress.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A second objection asks why multiple preexistent souls need distinct attributes: if attributes distinguish things, each attribute also needs distinguishing, producing circularity or infinite regress.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A third objection says souls might differ by essential properties; the proof that they share one species does not establish that they must.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A fourth objection allows preexistent souls to differ through accidents caused by matter, proposing that each might have been attached to an earlier body, and so on; excluding this requires disproving transmigration.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The discussion says Ghazālī's proof of the soul's origination then depends on refuting transmigration, while philosophers use origination to reject it; the proposed chain leads to two souls in one body and circularity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p42/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A fifth objection asks why, even without any previous body, souls could not differ by accidents, each caused by an earlier accident without a first one.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Potential souls first become distinct through attachment to particular receptacles; each then becomes aware of its own self, and that awareness persists, preserving distinction.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الغزالي والشيخ من الفلاسفة | reports | Al-Ghazali and the philosopher called the Shaykh hold souls are one species; Alusi says the Shaykh offered not even a doubt, much less a proof.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غيره | reports | Another proponent argues that if human souls share their nature yet differ by an essential constituent, they would be composite and therefore bodily.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Before bodies, a soul could not be distinct: awareness follows distinction, and no other distinguisher exists to precede that awareness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صاحب المعتبر | reports | The author of al-Muʿtabar argues that prebodily souls either transmigrated from earlier bodies, which we would remember, or were idle in nature; Alusi calls the whole argument very weak.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قدماء الفلاسفة | reports | Ancient philosophers argue that anything originated needs matter to make existence preferable to nonexistence; thus an originated soul would be material, which they deny.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قدماء الفلاسفة | reports | They argue that if souls began with bodies, infinitely many past bodies would entail infinitely many current souls, impossible because whatever admits increase and decrease is finite.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قدماء الفلاسفة | reports | They argue that originated things perish, whereas souls are everlasting by consensus, so souls must be eternal.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Alusi accepts that souls depend for origination on bodies, but rejects the inference that dependence means they are bodily inhering in them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The claim that finite souls follow from their ability to increase or decrease is not self-evident and requires proof; the argument works only for things capable of bodily extension or inherence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p43/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The philosophers give no proof for the premise that whatever is not eternal cannot be everlasting, so that premise is not accepted.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p44/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غيره | reports | A second argument for one soul-species says all people share capacities for knowledge and moral traits; since souls are known as perceiving and volitionally active, they are equal in all intelligible attributes.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p44/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غيره | reports | A third argument says every immaterial essence knows itself; Zayd's soul apprehends only an essence capable of cognition and volition, shared by all souls, so their full essence is one species.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p44/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Alusi rejects the first argument: souls might differ in species without sharing a genus, or share features as nonconstitutive concomitants; even essential composition need not be bodily.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The second same-species argument rests on inadequate induction: one cannot show every person receives every intelligible, or that a soul able to receive one attribute receives all attributes.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The third argument would make all separate beings one species, which Alusi says is untenable.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · شرذمة وصاحب المعتبر | reports | A small group holds that souls differ by species, and this is the position of the author of al-Muʿtabar.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صاحب المعتبر | reports | The best case for differing soul-species points to differences in knowledge, strength, anger, and forbearance despite similar temperaments, and prophetic power over universal matter not caused by temperament.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Alusi says the argument from personal differences and prophetic power is not a proof, only weak persuasion.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p45/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The angels' prostration to Adam may have been homage and honor, or prostration to God with Adam as the qibla where divine power's marvels appeared; Alusi cites Hassan's line about praying toward the qibla.

[ELMALILI:15:28-29/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God brings the clay to a complete human creation and an ordered human form.
[ELMALILI:15:28-29/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The possessive 'My spirit' is an honorific genitive that ennobles the spirit by its attribution to God.
[ELMALILI:15:28-29/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The phrase about breathing into Adam is figurative, not a literal account of divine breathing.
[ELMALILI:15:28-29/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God perfected matter's capacity and bestowed within it a spirit that is a divine command, as stated in 17:85. | mentions 17:85
[ELMALILI:15:28-29/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The angels prostrate in obedience to God, submitting to the spirit-bearing human whom God thereby elevated above clay.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The account of Adam is conjoined to another narrative; the opening idh is governed by an omitted 'remember,' as in parallel passages in al-Baqara and al-Aʿrāf.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Specifying the human's material teaches that a creature's honor comes from its qualities, not the substance from which it is composed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Taswiya is adjustment of a thing's constitution; here it is the balancing and completion of its elements until it can receive the spirit.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Blowing literally expels compressed air between pursed lips; here it metaphorically denotes the sudden placement of a subtle, powerfully acting force, with no actual blowing or blown object.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | As an approximation, life involves a rapidly formed vaporous or electrical force from the heart at the completion of bodily temperament, whose effects flow through arteries throughout the body.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Attributing the blowing and spirit to God's pronoun honors this creature.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p43/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage implies that elements are distinguished before God by their effects and actions; human notions of dirtiness or purity reflect sensory response, temperament, or custom.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر عليه السلام | reports | A report says the spirit was created by God and breathed into Adam from it.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو عبد الله عليه السلام | reports | God created a body and a spirit and ordered an angel to breathe into it; the spirit is from His power, not a part whose loss diminishes Him.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · سماعة | reports | Sama'a transmits the Imam's account that Adam was created and breathed into, and that the spirit is God's power from the realm of malakut.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The spirit is God's active power, emanating from His essential power, as the preceding report indicates.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر عليه السلام | reports | The spirit is a specially chosen and created spirit, attributed to God and preferred over all spirits, from which He ordered Adam to be breathed.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر عليه السلام | reports | In the report about Adam being created in God's image, the image is a created, originated form chosen above other forms and attributed to God as the Ka'ba is called His House.
[TABATABAI:15:26-48#3/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | These are exceptionally valuable reports on the spirit and contain extensive teachings that will be explained when the nature of spirit is discussed.
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Taswiyah means making something properly balanced and ordered, with each part in its proper place and condition; for a human, each organ is where and as it should be.
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The wording suggests the first human's body was created gradually: first its parts were assembled, then arranged in their fitting places and states, and then the spirit was breathed into it.
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | This gradual formation does not conflict with 3:59: its statement that God then said Be and it was concerns the soul's coming to be, not the body's formation. | mentions 3:59
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The author connects the body's gradual creation to 23:14, which describes the later creation of the human as another creation after the body was formed. | mentions 23:14
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Nafkh literally means putting air into a body through a mouth or otherwise, and can metaphorically mean imparting an intangible effect or command.
[TABATABAI:15:28-29/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Here the blowing signifies God's bringing the human spirit into existence in its relation to and attachment to the body, not air literally entering it.
[TABATABAI:15:29-33/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Reading 23:13–14, the human spirit is the body brought into being as a new creation while the body itself remains unchanged. | mentions 23:13, 23:14
[TABATABAI:15:29-33/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The spirit exists in itself, is united to the body through attachment, and is independent when that attachment ends at death; 32:11 says the spirit is taken while the body remains intact. | mentions 32:11
[TABATABAI:15:29-33/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī points back to his discussion of the spirit at 2:154 and promises a fuller treatment at 17:85. | mentions 2:154, 17:85
[TABATABAI:15:29-33/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The possessive construction my spirit is an ownership genitive used to honor and ennoble the spirit.
[TABATABAI:15:29-33/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | فَقَعُوا means prostrate; it may also evoke falling face-down, intensifying the angels’ submission to this new creature.
[ASAD-NOTES:15:26#n26/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The creation and prostration passages are allegorical: God's creation requires no elapsed time, since His will brings a thing into being immediately, as several verses affirm. | mentions 2:30-34, 7:11-18, 2:117, 3:47, 3:59, 6:73, 16:40, 19:35, 36:82, 40:68
[ASAD-NOTES:15:26#n26/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | God's breathing of His spirit is a metaphor for endowing man with life and consciousness, that is, with a soul.
[ASAD-NOTES:15:26/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | God forms mortal man fully, breathes spirit into him, and commands the angels to prostrate before him.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p279/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The command for the angels to prostrate preceded Adam's creation; they were to prostrate after he was perfected and God's spirit was breathed into him.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p279/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Human distinction rests on perfected abilities and the divine spark: preserving these merits the angels' prostration, while wasting them makes a person worse than an animal.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p279/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The divine spark is the source of spiritual advancement and connection with God when safeguarded; squandered, it leaves a person spiritually dark.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | After forming Adam's body and breathing spirit into him, God completed the first human's biological development and body-spirit unity, creating the most developed living kind.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r10] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · أحد كبار الصوفية | reports | A leading Sufi says every person inwardly harbors a claim to greatness like Pharaoh's declaration of being the greatest god, though unable to voice it.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r11] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Gazzâlî | reports | Ghazali says servitude weighs on the spirit while mastery is naturally loved; its longing for perfection never fades, and every being loves itself and its perfection and abhors nonexistence or loss of its qualities.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r12] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Gazzâlî | reports | Ghazali says humans see mastery over other beings as a form of perfection and desire it; mastery means power to influence, change, and control things for one's use.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r13] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Gazzâlî | reports | Ghazali says people exercise mastery by using beings they can use and learning about those they cannot; true rather than illusory perfection consists in knowledge, will, and power, also accepted as God's core attributes across religions and schools.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r14] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Human worth comes from the transcendent spirit breathed into the body, not from the body; people thus seek distinction, superiority, knowledge, mastery, freedom, and power.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r15] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | People often mistake the meaning and purpose of knowledge, freedom, and power and pursue illusory perfection; they need sound physical and metaphysical knowledge, freedom from transient passions, and the power to perfect both knowledge and

[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r16] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Adam's rank that warranted the angels' prostration derives from the transcendent identity of his spirit; God had explained this nature to the angels, who obeyed. | mentions 2:30, 2:33
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:15:29/r17] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Iblis ignored Adam's spiritual essence and origin, judging only by material comparison of Adam's earth-made body with his own fire-made being; this rebellion led to his expulsion from divine mercy and curse until the Resurrection.
